newsitem.title: UK: London stocks ends mixed after Wall Street rally.
newsitem.headline: London stocks ends mixed after Wall Street rally.

text.p: UK shares ended a nervy session mixed on Tuesday as uncertainty over interest rates was offset by another firm morning session on Wall Street.
The FTSE 100 index recovered from a near 30-point decline to finish the day 1.5 points higher at 4,195.5.

The Dow industrials average, which dropped 40 points at the U.S. start, was up 27 points by the London close with investors expressing relief that U.S. Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan had not directly warned of a near-term rate hike. "Greenspan's comments were seen as neutral-- no surprises," one dealer said.
Declines pipped advances by 55 to 44 with one unchanged.
The Fed chairman delivered an upbeat assessment of a U.S. economy that showed "few signs of the imbalances and inflationary tensions that have disrupted past expansions."
Although he warned of possible wage-driven inflation in the future, he told the U.S. Senate budget committee that wages had been held down by heightened job insecurity.

"He's not said anything the market didn't expect," said Gerard Lyons, economist at DKB International. "He gave no signs of an imminent rate hike but he will remain vigilant to inflationary pressures."
The Fed chief urged the abolition of capital gains tax on share purchases but did not repeat his warning against "irrational exuberance" which sent stocks reeling in December.
"No one really expected him to tell Wall Street it was out of control but his comments on capital gains tax gave the market a bit of a boost," the head of trading at a major investment bank said.

Greenspan's comments lifted bond markets off their earlier lows as well. The March long gilt ended 1/32 higher at 110-30/32 after a low of 110-16/32. The March T-bond was up 2/32 at 111 after a low of 110-6/32.

Talk of a near-term UK rate hike took its toll on market confidence during the morning session after Bank of England governor Eddie George said interest rates needed to rise to curb inflationary pressures building in the British economy.
George's assertion late Monday that there were "real dangers" in letting sterling strength delay a rate rise rekindled market speculation that UK rates could go up in early February.
"The market is pretty much resigned to the fact that UK rates are going to have to go up sooner or later," the trader said.
"The only question is whether or not (UK Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth) Clarke will be able to hold off raising rates ahead of the (general) election."
Clarke's ruling Conservative party is trailing the opposition Labour by around 20 percentage points in opinion polls ahead of the election which must take place by May 22.
The strong pound has started to hit UK export orders according to the latest industrial trends survey from the Confederation of British Industry.
British manufactured exports have levelled off for the first time since October 1993, the CBI said.
"The impact of sterling's strength is beginning to feed through to manufacturers' export orders," said Ross Buckland, a member of the CBI's economic affairs committee.
Sterling's strength continued to spook market analysts. Broker ABN AMRO Hoare Govett cut profits forecasts for Associated British Foods, blaming the soaring pound.
ABF shares lost 3 to 482-1/2 pence.
Elsewhere, Mid Kent Water plunged 60 pence to 572-1/2 after the British government blocked a proposed takeover bid for the water company.
-- Dale Faulken, London Newsroom +44 171 542 7717
